lessons.title: Hello Python: the REPL and scripts
lessons.body:
## Interpreted and interactive

Python runs top-to-bottom. The **REPL** (`python`) lets you experiment line by line; scripts run with `python app.py`.

## No boilerplate

No class or main required. The common entry guard is `if __name__ == "__main__":` so a file can be both imported and run.

## Indentation is syntax

Blocks are defined by indentation (4 spaces), not braces. Consistency is mandatory.

codeSamples.title: Script entry

lessons.title: Variables, numbers, and dynamic typing
lessons.body:
## Dynamic but strong

Variables are names bound to objects; types live on the object, not the name. Python won't silently coerce `"1" + 1`.

## Numbers

`int` has arbitrary precision (no overflow). `float` is IEEE-754. Use `//` for floor division, `%` for remainder, `**` for power.

## Truthiness

Empty containers, `0`, `""`, and `None` are falsy; most other values are truthy.

codeSamples.title: Numeric ops
codeSamples.code:
big = 2 ** 100          # arbitrary precision
q, r = divmod(17, 5)     # (3, 2)
price = 19.99
name = "Corgi"

lessons.title: Strings and f-strings
lessons.body:
## Immutable text

Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode. Slicing (`s[1:4]`), `split`, `join`, `strip`, and `replace` cover most work.

## f-strings

The modern way to format: `f"Hi {name}, total {total:.2f}"`. They also support `=` for debugging: `f"{x=}"`.

## Bytes vs str

`str` is text; `bytes` is raw data. Encode/decode explicitly with UTF-8 at I/O boundaries.

codeSamples.title: f-string formatting
codeSamples.code:
name, total = "Ada", 19.5
print(f"Hi {name}, total ${total:.2f}")
print(f"{total=}")  # total=19.5

lessons.title: Control flow and match
lessons.body:
## if/elif/else

Clean conditionals with no parentheses required. Chained comparisons work: `0 < x < 10`.

## Loops

`for x in iterable` and `while`. Use `enumerate` for indices and `zip` to iterate in parallel. `break`, `continue`, and the rarely-used loop `else`.

## Structural pattern matching

`match/case` (Python 3.10+) destructures values and shapes — more than a switch.

codeSamples.title: match statement
codeSamples.code:
match command.split():
    case ["go", direction]:
        move(direction)
    case ["quit"]:
        stop()
    case _:
        print("unknown")

lessons.title: Lists, tuples, sets, and dicts
lessons.body:
## The four workhorses

- `list` — ordered, mutable.
- `tuple` — ordered, immutable (great as fixed records / dict keys).
- `set` — unique, unordered.
- `dict` — key/value, insertion-ordered since 3.7.

## Idioms

`d.get(k, default)`, `d.setdefault`, membership with `in` (O(1) for set/dict). Unpack with `a, b = pair`.

codeSamples.title: Dict counting

lessons.title: Comprehensions and generators
lessons.body:
## Comprehensions

Build lists/sets/dicts concisely: `[x*x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]`. Readable and fast.

## Generator expressions

Swap `[]` for `()` to get a **lazy** generator that yields items one at a time — memory-friendly for large data.

## Don't overdo it

Nested, side-effecting comprehensions hurt readability. A plain loop is sometimes clearer.

codeSamples.title: Comprehension + generator

lessons.title: Functions, args, and defaults
lessons.body:
## Flexible signatures

Positional, keyword, `*args`, and `**kwargs`. Keyword-only args come after `*`; positional-only before `/`.

## Default gotcha

Never use a mutable default (`def f(x=[])`) — it is created once and shared. Use `None` and create inside.

## Docstrings

The first string in a function is its docstring, surfaced by `help()` and tools.

codeSamples.title: Safe default

lessons.title: Modules, packages, and virtualenvs
lessons.body:
## Imports

A `.py` file is a module; a directory with modules is a package. Prefer explicit imports (`from pkg.mod import thing`).

## Isolation

Use a virtual environment per project so dependencies don't collide. `python -m venv .venv` then activate.

## Modern tooling

`uv` creates envs and installs deps at Rust speed, replacing much of pip/venv/pyenv friction.

codeSamples.title: Create and use an env
codeSamples.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install httpx
# or: uv venv && uv pip install httpx

lessons.title: Exceptions and context managers
lessons.body:
## EAFP

Python prefers "easier to ask forgiveness than permission": try the operation and catch failures rather than pre-checking.

## try/except/else/finally

Catch specific exceptions, use `else` for the success path, `finally` for cleanup. Re-raise with bare `raise`.

## with

Context managers (`with open(...) as f:`) guarantee cleanup. Write your own with `contextlib.contextmanager`.

codeSamples.title: with + specific except

lessons.title: Classes, dunder methods, and properties
lessons.body:
## Objects

Define `__init__` for construction; `self` is the instance. Methods are functions with `self` first.

## Dunder methods

Special methods power syntax: `__repr__`, `__eq__`, `__len__`, `__iter__`. Implement `__repr__` for debuggable objects.

## Properties

`@property` exposes computed attributes without breaking the `obj.attr` interface — no Java-style getters.

codeSamples.title: Class with property

lessons.title: Dataclasses and namedtuples
lessons.body:
## Less boilerplate

`@dataclass` generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__` from annotated fields — Python's value object.

## Defaults and immutability

Provide defaults, use `field(default_factory=list)` for mutable ones, and `frozen=True` for immutable records.

## When to use what

`NamedTuple` for lightweight immutable tuples; dataclass for richer mutable/immutable records; Pydantic when you need validation.

codeSamples.title: Dataclass

lessons.title: Iterators, generators, and yield
lessons.body:
## The iterator protocol

Anything with `__iter__`/`__next__` is iterable. `for` loops and comprehensions consume iterators.

## yield

A function with `yield` is a generator — it pauses and resumes, producing values lazily. Great for streams and pipelines.

## itertools

`chain`, `islice`, `groupby`, `count`, and `product` compose iterators efficiently without building intermediate lists.

codeSamples.title: Generator function

lessons.title: Decorators and closures
lessons.body:
## Functions are objects

You can pass, return, and nest functions. A **closure** captures variables from its enclosing scope.

## Decorators

A decorator wraps a function to add behavior (logging, caching, timing). Use `functools.wraps` to preserve metadata.

## Handy stdlib decorators

`@functools.cache`/`lru_cache` memoize, `@property`, `@staticmethod`, and `@dataclass` are all decorators.

codeSamples.title: Timing decorator

lessons.title: Type hints and static checking
lessons.body:
## Gradual typing

Type hints are optional and not enforced at runtime, but tools like **mypy**/**pyright** check them. They document intent and catch bugs.

## Modern syntax

Use builtin generics (`list[int]`, `dict[str, int]`), `X | None` unions, and PEP 695 type parameters (`def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T`).

## Protocols

`typing.Protocol` gives structural (duck) typing you can type-check — accept anything with the right shape.

codeSamples.title: Typed function + Protocol

lessons.title: Standard library essentials
lessons.body:
## Batteries included

- `pathlib.Path` for filesystem paths.
- `collections`: `defaultdict`, `Counter`, `deque`.
- `datetime` + `zoneinfo` for timezone-aware times.
- `json`, `csv`, `re` for data.

## Prefer stdlib

Reach for the standard library before adding a dependency — it's audited, stable, and dependency-free.

codeSamples.title: Counter and Path
codeSamples.code:
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

text = Path("poem.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
top = Counter(text.split()).most_common(3)

lessons.title: Testing with pytest
lessons.body:
## Plain functions

pytest discovers `test_*.py` files and `test_*` functions. Just use `assert` — pytest rewrites it for rich output.

## Fixtures

`@pytest.fixture` provides reusable setup (temp dirs, DB sessions) with teardown via `yield`.

## Parametrize

`@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs a test across many inputs — Python's table-driven testing.

codeSamples.title: Parametrized test

lessons.title: Files, JSON, and serialization
lessons.body:
## pathlib first

`Path.read_text` / `write_text` handle small files. For large data, iterate line by line to bound memory.

## JSON

`json.loads`/`dumps` round-trip Python dicts. Use `default=` for custom types and `indent=` for readable output.

## Encoding discipline

Always pass `encoding="utf-8"`; never rely on the platform default, which differs across OSes.

codeSamples.title: JSON round-trip
codeSamples.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path

data = json.loads(Path("in.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
Path("out.json").write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

lessons.title: Types, Pydantic v2, uv, and Ruff
lessons.body:
## Types

PEP 695 type params, `Protocol`, and strict type checkers (pyright/mypy) are expected on serious teams.

## Pydantic v2

Rust core — much faster. Prefer `Annotated` constraints and settings via `pydantic-settings`.

## Tooling

`uv` replaces a lot of pip/poetry/pyenv friction. `Ruff` covers lint + format at Rust speed.

## GIL note

Free-threading is experimental in recent CPython — know what it means, don't assume production readiness everywhere.

codeSamples.title: Pydantic model
codeSamples.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)

lessons.title: Logging and configuration
lessons.body:
## Never print in production

Use the `logging` module: leveled, configurable, and routable to files/services. Get a module-level logger with `logging.getLogger(__name__)`.

## Levels

`DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL`. Configure once at startup with `basicConfig` or `dictConfig`; libraries should only emit, not configure.

## Structured logs

Emit key/value context (request id, user) for searchable logs. `logger.exception` inside an `except` captures the traceback.

codeSamples.title: Module logger

lessons.title: async/await fundamentals
lessons.body:
## Cooperative concurrency

`async def` defines a coroutine; `await` yields control while waiting on I/O. A single thread juggles thousands of awaits.

## Running

`asyncio.run(main())` starts the event loop. `await` only inside `async` functions.

## The trap

Calling a blocking function (`requests`, `time.sleep`) inside a coroutine stalls the whole loop. Use async libraries or `run_in_executor`.

codeSamples.title: Basic coroutine
codeSamples.code:
import asyncio, httpx

async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        r = await client.get("https://example.com")
        print(r.status_code)

asyncio.run(main())

lessons.title: FastAPI: async def vs def
lessons.body:
## The production footgun

`async def` is not automatically faster. Use `async def` when you **await** async I/O. If the body calls blocking libraries (`requests`, sync ORM, `time.sleep`), prefer plain `def` so FastAPI offloads to a thread pool — or you will block the event loop.

## Stack

FastAPI + Pydantic v2 + SQLAlchemy 2.0 async + asyncpg is the common 2026 API stack. Keep create/update/response schemas separate so secrets never leak.

## Background work

`BackgroundTasks` for quick follow-ups. Celery/Arq for heavy or retryable jobs.

codeSamples.title: Route style choice

lessons.title: TaskGroup, pools, and connection math
lessons.body:
## TaskGroup vs gather

`asyncio.TaskGroup` cancels siblings on failure (structured concurrency). Prefer it for related tasks.

## Connection pools

One async worker can multiplex thousands of requests. Size DB pools relative to workers × concurrent awaits, or you'll hit `too many connections`.

## CPU-bound

Offload to processes/queues — threads still contend on the GIL for pure Python CPU work.

codeSamples.title: TaskGroup
codeSamples.code:
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tg.create_task(fetch(a))
    tg.create_task(fetch(b))

lessons.title: The GIL, threads, and processes
lessons.body:
## What the GIL does

CPython's Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help **I/O-bound** work (they release the GIL while waiting).

## CPU-bound work

Use `multiprocessing` or `concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor` to use multiple cores, or push hot loops into NumPy/C extensions.

## Free-threading

Python 3.13+ ships an experimental no-GIL build. Know it exists, but don't assume ecosystem/library readiness in production yet.

codeSamples.title: Process pool for CPU work
codeSamples.code:
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(crunch, chunks))

lessons.title: Packaging and publishing
lessons.body:
## pyproject.toml

The single source of truth for metadata, dependencies, and build config. `uv`, `hatch`, and `pip` all read it.

## Building and publishing

`python -m build` creates a wheel + sdist; `twine upload` (or `uv publish`) pushes to PyPI. Pin a compatible Python range.

## Reproducibility

Lock dependencies (`uv.lock`/`requirements.txt`) for apps; keep libraries' constraints loose. Separate dev and runtime deps.

codeSamples.title: pyproject essentials
codeSamples.code:
[project]
name = "corgi-cli"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = ["httpx>=0.27"]

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

lessons.title: Profiling and performance
lessons.body:
## Measure, don't guess

Profile with `cProfile`/`pstats` or `py-spy` (sampling, no code change). Find the real hot path before optimizing.

## Common wins

Use the right data structure (set for membership), avoid quadratic loops, cache with `functools.lru_cache`, and vectorize numeric work with NumPy.

## Micro-benchmark

`timeit` for small snippets. Beware premature optimization — readable code first, then optimize the measured bottleneck.

codeSamples.title: Profile a call
codeSamples.code:
import cProfile, pstats
cProfile.run("main()", "out.prof")
pstats.Stats("out.prof").sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(10)
